posts.description:
AI Agents Just Became Multiplayer. Here's How to Build Them.

I've spent months building my own AI OS with skills, memory, and connections to the tools I use every day.

But when everyone on the team builds their own setup, we end up duplicating integrations and passing context between tools.

So we're testing Kylon with a small part of our team, where humans, Claude Code, and Codex can work together in the same rooms.

→ My teammates can talk to the same agents I use.
→ Our agents can message each other and collaborate on work.
→ Each room has its own apps, automations, and files.

One of the first things I built was a weekly commitments tracker with a daily agent check-in.

We were finishing work in ClickUp and forgetting to mark it complete, so my AI OS thought someone had finished one out of eight tasks when they'd actually finished four.

That's a pretty practical place to start: helping the team keep the tools we already use accurate.

We're trying this with one small business unit first, then adding another workflow once we've got a process that works.

Link to the full video is in the comments 👇

posts.description:
One of the most interesting uses of AI may be solving the cold start problem in networks.

Because in multiplayer games, the hardest thing to create is not always the map, the characters, or the economy.

It is the room full of players that makes the game worth playing.

That was one of my favorite takeaways from hosting my friend Akhil Jindal, cofounder of Moku, in my Generative AI class at The Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School.

We often talk about AI-generated content as if "content" means text, images, video, or code. But in games, other players are part of the content. They create the unpredictability, competition, coordination, and social energy that make the world feel alive.

That makes multiplayer gaming a fascinating AI problem.

If there are not enough players, the game has a cold start problem.

If there are rewards, especially in crypto gaming, bots show up to extract value.

Akhil's team is exploring a different path by using reinforcement learning to train AI agents that can play games. Not because every AI product needs an LLM, but because sometimes the thing you need to generate is behavior.

That creates a useful shift in framing.

What if AI agents are not just NPCs or adversaries, but part of the early player network that helps a game become playable, testable, and resilient?

Of course, that opens up a deeper product question.

How do you design a game that works for both humans and AI?

That changes how you think about mechanics, incentives, difficulty, testing, trust, and even what "fun" means.

A big thank you to Akhil for joining us at Carey and giving students a practical look at how AI products get built in the real world.

posts.description:
Using AI is a lot like a video game, you're either in single-player or multiplayer.

We're seeing a lot of people play one while thinking they're in the other.

In single-player, the AI works next to you as a copilot, drafting the email that goes out from your address under your name.

In multiplayer, the agent is more like a teammate with its own accounts and its own inbox. It sends the email from its own address and loops you in when it needs a decision.

One acts as you, the other acts as itself.

The problems can start small: the copilot drafts a reply to a customer, it looks fine, and you send it after a skim.

A few weeks in, it's doing more of the thinking, and you're doing less of the reading, and the customer still assumes every word came from you.

At that point, you're treating a copilot like an agent, but with your name still on the work. This is a slippery slope for many: it's easy to become a "meat proxy" that blindly uses AI.

Both ways of working with AI do well when you pick one on purpose.

Either you own the words and check them, or the agent owns them, and you coach it.

I've leaned toward multiplayer for most of my own work, since an agent with its own identity has been easier to secure and to coach.

comments.text:
Agreed. Most work isn't individual; it’s handoffs—the order moving from sales to ops to the carrier, the call a manager never hears, the approval waiting on someone else's reply.

Most AI tools are built for one person and one chat window. In business, the cost sits in the gaps between people. A shared AI workforce is useful only if it knows who owns each step and what the next person needs to see.

Multiplayer is less about more people in the chat and more about AI sitting in the handoff, where work actually stalls.

Fable 5.1 is going to change everything. I made https://fledglinggame.com.

I put GitHub Copilot in autopilot and fed it a single prompt - generate a fully functional first-person multiplayer game where you play as a baby bird learning to fly...

"Your task is to build a first person (chase camera) multi-player game where the user plays as a baby bird leaving the nest and exploring a bucolic countryside rich with interactions, structures, games and delightful discoveries. This game should be visually stunning such that it draws the user in and makes them never want to leave. Test all your work and do not stop until you have created a "breath of the wild" caliber visual experience. Everything should run in the browser."

I've added a bunch of features since the initial prompt but so much of what you see in that video was from the initial one shot.

And because I think if you're going to make claims like I just did, you gotta publish your work...

Full disclosure that I have no idea what will happen if too many people join at once. It's on the cheapest possible hosting tier. I also have not tested on all hardware so no clue if your machine can handle it or not. But let's find out.

posts.transcript: Welcome to single player to multiplayer context through collaboration. I'm John Cutler, and you can find me on LinkedIn. Imagine a world where ordinary people discover a superpower. At first it's disorienting, ambiguous, and a huge dopamine hit. It feels like everything is possible, but soon there is pressure to use this power just to keep up. This power, called the signal, is accessible to everyone, but it comes from a powerful organization known as the Lattice. The Lattice benefits when people believe the power is individual, reinforcing the message that they need the signal to preserve their influence. As individuals start wielding the signal, people turn inward, trusting the power more than each other. Collaborators become competitors, fighting their own battles in a single player game. Even as the power intensifies, what was once exhilarating turns into constant anxiety and nonstop hard decisions. The space for intuition and collaboration disappears, replaced by constant decisions, prompts, and switching. This feels like progress, but pulls people further into single player mode. The more you rely on the signal, the more you risk dependence on the lattice. Your native abilities atrophy and only the most experienced can see where the illusion ends. Their expertise is becoming increasingly rare. Zooming out, entire alliances are forming, but distrust is rising. Mechanisms intended for shared clarity are used to control from a distance. The tension is building will be continue as solo superheroes or coordinate like a team to step into a multiplayer mode. We are at the beginning of this story. The powers are discovered, the stakes are clear, and the tension is rising. The critical question for all of us is will we keep playing? This is a single player game. Or figure out what it means to do this together. My observations show 2 paths. On one side, thoughtful systems thinkers are using AI to catalyst multiplayer mode, reducing cognitive load and creating space for collaboration and shared context. On the other side, overwhelm is growing. Highly pathological dynamics are pushing people into more single player mode. Endless work in progress and constant demands are amplified by AI, with overload feeling like the job itself. I don't have a single answer, but I want to offer a few frames to make sense of what is happening. My goal is to give us a shared language so our conversations can go a level deeper In one model, context is portable and owned by individuals, but the reality is that context is produced through interaction. It arises through engagement in both parties are changed by it, with context flowing outward from the interaction. The Shannon Weaver model sees understanding as a function of message, context and noise. Populist AI models frame it as a function of prompt context and model, suggesting context is a universal solvent for clarity, however. The 4E model of cognition reminds us that understanding is not passive reconstruction. It is a function of agents, bodies, environment, and interaction, meaning it happens through active engagement in a shared situation. Boyd's OODA loop shows that orientation shaped by context and interaction is key. True understanding forms and reforms as people engage with each other and the situation, not by preloading or transferring information. If understanding is generated through interaction, 3 things matter how interaction works. Which involves the four's what this requires from us, involving the three meta cognitions and when this matters as not every problem needs the same level of interaction. The 4E model of cognition, embodied, embedded, extended and inactive emerged as a counter to the idea that thinking happens only in the head. It shows that understanding is not just processing information, but emerges through interaction. Embodied cognition means thinking is constrained by sensory motor coupling. It's about contact with reality. Understanding comes from engaging with. Something not just representing it. Embedded cognition means thinking depends on environmental structure and affordances, shaping what you notice and how you reason. It's about the structure of the situation. Extended cognition means thinking spreads across tools and other agents, meaning the system is doing the thinking, not just the individual. It's about where thinking is distributed. In active cognition means understanding arises through dynamic interaction. It's where understanding actually emerges through continuous engagement and action. Embodied grounds us in reality. Embedded shapes what we see, extended spreads thinking across systems and inactive is where understanding actually emerges. The broadcast model treats communication as a transmission problem where understanding is decoding. Commanders intent assumes alignment emerges through interaction with the situation, not by decoding a message. If understanding is generated through interaction, what capabilities do people need to do it well? Metacognition or thinking about your own thinking is important for monitoring, understanding and regulating problem solving. Social metacognition, thinking about other people's thinking, is crucial for teams to coordinate better and avoid misalignment, especially with AI in the loop. Computational metacognition involves thinking about how AI works and what it is optimizing for. Better mental models of AI lead to better questions, error detection, and calibrated trust. Without the ability to reason about your own thinking, others thinking, and the AI's purpose, you will struggle to use AI effectively where shared understanding is needed in the movie context Stark and Banner created. Patron was strong individual metacognition but without collective sense. Making the missing interaction gap led to a failed outcome. When Steve Rogers pushed for alignment, they brought their thinking back into the group. The thinking then happened across people, allowing them to make sense of the situation together. Not all work requires the same level of interaction. The mistake is treating every problem and decision like the same kind of fight when sometimes little situational awareness is needed. We can imagine a two by three matrix for different situations. On one axis we have context full or context. Right on the other, we borrow from Cinnabon with clear, complicated and complex categories. Each cell requires a different motion. In the clear context light space, cause and effect are stable, instructions are enough, and context is minimal. AI can provide full automation and coordination is minimal. An example is bulk invoice processing. In the clear context, full space context is known and supplied, but definitions and permissions matter. Coordination is light. AI acts as a retrieval grounded assistant, injecting local context. This is like support teams resolving tickets with shared playbooks and the complicated context light space. The work is multi step and predictable, requiring planning and expertise. Collaboration is sequenced with clear roles. AI can act as a planner or copilot, optimizing workflows. This applies to defined product development processes in the complicated context. Full space context is distributed, requiring ongoing high coordination across teams and systems. AI is a workflow orchestrator, navigating permissions and keeping things In Sync and. Example is launching a feature across multiple departments. In the complex context light space problems are hard but solvable independently driven by structure, not social factors. Coordination is low. AI is a research engine or strategy generator with high cognitive power and low situational coupling. In the complex context full space, there is ambiguity, constraints and politics. With knowledge evolving. Interaction and coordination are maximum. AI acts as a sense making partner, not a decision engine. This describes leadership aligning. Strategy during a market shift. The big picture is that you cannot use the same AI practices in all contexts. As the situation becomes more dynamic and the rate of context generation increases, your approach must adapt. There are two different ways to interpret AI's impact. The optimistic view sees AI's a catalyst for collaboration and shared context, closing the gap where old tools failed to capture meaning and context. The pessimistic view sees AI as a catalyst for legibility and control, shifting from Messi distributed understanding to clean centralized. Single player views. The question is whether AI strengthens multiplayer understanding or collapses it into single player control.

comments.text:
Jeff, the roadmap toward agents and worlds learning together raises a game-design question I care about: how does a player tell that a companion has learned, while still being able to trust the world's rules?
For a future cooperative task, I'd test a human and an agent learning to cover each other's retreat. Save checkpoints of both the policy and world model, then cross-test old/new policies against old/new worlds, with held-out human partners. That helps separate better coordination from a simulator change that simply makes the task easier. Where a reference environment is available, I'd also check whether the behavior survives there.
Success rate alone would miss part of the experience. I'd record whether the agent leaves its partner stranded, recovers when the partner changes plans, and gives the human room to contribute.
For persistent AI companions, that distinction matters: growing together should create new ways to cooperate that players can recognize and rely on. Is evaluating this kind of transferable cooperation part of the direction beyond the current combat preview?

Introducing Agora-2, our next-generation multi-agent world model!

Agora-2 supports up to 20 humans and agents interacting inside a shared environment, all simulated in real time.

Our multiplayer research preview is available to try right now. This research preview of Agora-2 enables up to 4 humans to join together to battle 16 agents, in an environment simulated in real time by the world model. There's no game engine under the hood.

Going forward, we believe multi-agent world models will increasingly power important applications across AI training, AI safety, robotics, autonomous vehicles, defense, energy, cybersecurity, and gaming.

Experience Agora-2 right now!

comments.text:
The key idea behind MultiGen is a shared external memory that represents the world state across players.

The memory stores the map layout and active player poses, while each player runs their own Observation and Dynamics modules and reads from the same shared state. This structure is what makes multiplayer natural and, importantly, lets us train a multiplayer model using only data from a single view.

A nice consequence of external memory is that it makes level design natural.

Because the environment is defined explicitly through a top-down map layout, users can create and edit the world before inference starts, and the model generates first-person observations that stay consistent with that structure.

Project page: https://ryanpo.com/multigen/
Paper: https://ryanpo.com/multigen/static/pdfs/multigen.pdf

posts.description:
Video world models are real-time MULTIPLAYER game engines!

Introducing MultiGen - a real-time multiplayer game generated entirely by a neural network. MultiGen is a real-time multiplayer diffusion game engine that supports an arbitrary number of players (not just 2!) through a shared memory-based world model.

Single-player world models can already be entertaining, but things get much more interesting once the experience becomes shared. MultiGen extends diffusion-based gameplay to real-time multiplayer, where players interact through a common generated world rather than separate isolated rollouts. Here’s a 30-minute timelapse of 4-player gameplay running in real time.

Project page: https://lnkd.in/g8yviiK6
Paper: https://lnkd.in/gREv3JVM

comments.text: The approval react is the part that decides whether this scales or quietly becomes a rubber stamp. I have run versions of this inside enterprise teams and the failure mode is approval fatigue, by week three people stop reading the draft and just hit the check, which is worse than no gate because now nobody owns the mistake. What held up was promoting tasks from draft-only to auto-complete only after the agent cleared 20 clean runs on that exact task type. Curious how you decide what graduates out of the high-risk bucket, time, error rate, or gut?
comments.author: Anees Merchant

comments.text: The loop-per-person structure is a tidy solve for the handoff problem. Most teams experimenting with AI end up with parallel setups where each person has their own workflow and nothing joins up. Routing through a shared channel with a Chief of Staff layer that knows context across the team is how you get compound value rather than just individual efficiency gains.

posts.description:
AI agents shouldn't run in single player mode.

So we changed it.

Most people work in teams, but the more individualistic AI usage gets, the more gatekept its power becomes. So we built agent workforce loops — now my teammates can prompt each other's AI agents (image below).

How it works (we’re still iterating!):
- Each core teammate gets a "loop" Slack channel (ex: loop-allie)
- Teammates + Claude Code/Codex are in it
- Anyone can drop a task in the chat
- Low-risk: my AI Chief of Staff routes it, completes it, verifies, reacts ✅
- Higher-risk (sending emails, pulling files): it preps but stops, drafts only
- I approve by reacting ✅
- The whole workforce runs on a 15-min loop

Essentially: teammates can prompt another teammate's AI agent workforce.
